name: Collar and shirt choice for thick neck

lead: This is a style practice: people with thick necks choose collar shapes such as spread, point, button-down or mandarin, and shirt fits that frame the neck and show it to its best effect. The change in look is immediate when worn.
Collar shape frames the neck and jaw visually and affects how a shirt sits. Collar types are well documented as general descriptions; there is no research on how they change perceived neck size.

paras: People try different collar shapes, check that the shirt fits properly at the neck, and choose the one that balances neck and shoulders. It costs only the price of the shirts and can be adjusted by tailoring.
No health risks are documented. A shirt that is too tight at the neck is generally regarded as uncomfortable.

web.title: Dress shirts for men with a thick neck

angle.text: Picking a collar shape such as spread, point, button-down or mandarin, with a suitable shirt fit, frames a thick neck and shows it to its best effect. The change in look is immediate when the shirt is worn.

lead: Collar and shirt choice for a thick neck is a clothing practice in which men with a larger neck, often from neck training, lifting or build, select collar shapes and shirt cuts so that shirts sit comfortably and look balanced around the neck and shoulders. A collar that fits well avoids the pinched, tight look at the neck and keeps the shirt proportioned, so the neck reads as a strong feature rather than as strained fabric [1][2].

Shirt collars come in several standard shapes: spread, point, button-down, band (mandarin) and others [3][1]. Menswear retailers that address thick necks describe wide-spaced collars such as the cutaway as a common choice, because the widely spaced points open the neck visually, and they say that narrow, short-pointed collars and no-fold band collars can crowd it [2].

Sizing is part of the practice. Dress shirts are sized by neck circumference and sleeve length, and shirts for neck sizes around 18 inches or more may be sold under "Big" or "Portly" labels [1]. No published study has tested how collar shape changes perceived neck size or attractiveness.

paras: Wikipedia categorises collars as standing, turnover or flat, and lists named shirt styles [3]. A spread collar has a wide gap between the points and can accommodate a bulky tie knot, while a point collar has long pointed edges usually worn with a suit and tie, and a button-down collar fastens its points to the shirt body [3]. A dress shirt article gives spread collars as measuring about 3.5 to 8.5 inches between the points, with the widest versions called cutaway or Windsor collars, and point collars as about 2.5 to 4 inches [1].
The Wikipedia collar article says little about neck proportions; its one relevant example is that Elvis Presley favoured an upturned collar because he thought his neck looked too long [3].

Neck size is a circumference measured from the centre of the top button to the centre of the buttonhole, and US ready-to-wear dress shirts list neck size and sleeve length as two numbers such as 15.5 and 34 [1]. Neck and sleeve sizes ignore chest and waist, so some shirts are cut fuller for larger midsections, and fitted, tailored, athletic and trim cuts exist alongside classic cuts [1].

A French custom-shirt retailer places the thick-neck threshold at about 16.5 inches (42 cm), against an adult average of about 14 to 17 inches. It says ready-to-wear shirts are cut as one block, so going up a size for the collar also enlarges the chest, shoulders and sleeves, which it calls the "parachute effect", while custom shirts size the neck independently [2]. As a seller of custom shirts, it has a commercial interest in this explanation.

The same retailer says a cutaway collar is its default for a thick neck, a classic forward-point collar works if the band is sized correctly, a button-down is acceptable but short-point versions crowd the neck, and band (mandarin) collars fit snugly at the neck base with no opening [2].

Clothing and fit are treated as part of style presentation in appearance communities, alongside grooming and body composition. No community threads specifically on collars for thick necks were available to document specific claims.
